articles.title: F1 in Rwanda: Why deal for race in Africa is also controversial
articles.summary: Formula 1 will return to Africa in the early 2030s, but Rwanda's deal to stage a race has prompted accusations of sportswashing against the country.
articles.body:
Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time in a generation after Rwanda agreed a 10-year contract to stage a race, with the sport's governing body (FIA) keen to create a "lasting legacy".

The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, with the first edition in the "early 2030s".

For Rwandan President Paul Kagame, the ambition is to "pave the way" for other F1 races on the continent.

However, the announcement has drawn criticism from some quarters amid allegations of sportswashing and questions around the East African country's human rights record.

Africa has not hosted an F1 race since 1993, and the clamour to return to the continent has been growing in recent years - with seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton among those leading the calls.

Morocco was the first African nation to host a Grand Prix in 1958 and 23 races were then held in South Africa between 1962 and 1993.

President Kagame said it was "an honour and privilege" for Rwanda to be chosen for its return.

"This partnership is long overdue but it is a success and a milestone for the entire continent - especially for African fans," he added.

South Africa had been keen to secure its own F1 race, and sports minister Gayton McKenzie remains bullish about his country's hopes of emulating Rwanda.

"They have worked on it longer than SA and deserve it," he posted on X.

"Remember though that one country, Italy, has had two [F1 races] a year, and some react like a continent of [54] countries can only get one. SA will get F1, even before 2030."

Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993

A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?

The year of the first African Grand Prix in the 2030s, and its timing in the calendar, are yet to be announced.

F1 is likely to want to avoid holding the race in Rwanda's main rainy season of March to May, while there is a shorter, less disruptive, rainy season from October to November.

The sport is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.

Former F1 driver Alex Wurz will be involved in the design of the circuit, which is due to use the undulating Rwandan landscape to produce a track with a natural flow and elevation changes of nearly 200m to challenge drivers.

Could the race boost African participation?

Jody Sheckter remains the only African to win the F1 Drivers' Championship, triumphing in 1979 with Ferrari.

"It's so expensive to get in," the South African told Newsday on the BBC World Service when discussing whether or not the race in Rwanda could open the door to more drivers from the continent.

"I built my own cars at the beginning. You can't do that anymore."

Africans hoping for a career in motorsport have previously had to chase their dream overseas, according to fellow driver Axcil Jefferies, who has previously competed in Formula 2.

But the Zimbabwean believes that could now change.

"F1 coming to Africa will highlight to everyone what a big industry motorsport is," he said.

"All the elements will inspire the youth, whether that's to come in as an engineer, as a mechanic, as drivers, as team coordinators."

South African presenter Kriya Gangiah, who hosts SuperSport's F1 Extra Africa Trackside podcast, is also hopeful of a boost in the number of female fans and drivers in Africa.

"The more you see something and the more that is present in your world, the more you take interest in it," she said.

"Being in paddocks in South Africa, you're seeing the amount of women that are making it into the sport and are actually doing really well. A lot of the girls are giving the guys a proper run for their money."

Allegations of sportswashing - hosting sporting events to improve a country's international reputation - have long been levelled against Rwanda.

Securing an F1 race is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment.

The country has hosted the Basketball Africa League finals in all but one year since 2021 and staged cycling's World Road Championships last year, the first time the event had been held in Africa.

Visit Rwanda has either sponsored or had partnerships with Arsenal, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain, although its sleeve sponsorship of the Gunners ended this year after drawing criticism from supporter groups.

Meanwhile, Rwanda's central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.

Human Rights Watch previously said that "the space for freedom of expression" and "political autonomy" is shrinking in the country.

"Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record," said Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns Felix Jakens.

"A 10-year Grand Prix 'presented by Visit Rwanda' is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities."

The Rwandan government has dismissed such accusations, with chief tourism officer Irene Murerwa calling them "a distraction' from the "amazing and outstanding achievements the country has made" when previously challenged by BBC Sport Africa.

"The benefits trickle down to every Rwandan," she said in December 2024. "Hosting F1 would be another step in our journey to becoming a world-class destination."

F1 is not blind to issues around sportswashing, with several countries on the calendar accused of utilising the strategy - not least Saudi Arabia.

F1's own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders.

A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."

However, it has still drawn criticism from human rights organisations, with Amnesty International's Jakens believing the organisation's words "ring hollow".

"It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise," he said.

When asked about the sportswashing accusations levelled against Rwanda when it was bidding to host a race, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem told BBC Sport Africa: "When people cannot get what they want, they always blame it on sportswashing.

"I honestly don't care about what they say."

articles.title: Quiles: "No he venido al Mundial a ganar un título y ya está”
articles.standfirst: Entrevista MARCA al campeón de Moto3
articles.summary: Entrevista MARCA al campeón de Moto3
articles.body: Agotado, pero con la sonrisa instalada en su cara de forma perenne. Así estaba Máximo Quiles (Murcia, 2008), recién aterrizado de Indonesia, donde se proclamó campeón de Moto3. El ‘Gladiator’ lo festejó a lo grande incluso con Marc Márquez, su mentor. Ahora, le esperan nuevos retos, pero los afronta con la misma ambición. PREGUNTA. Ya todo el mundo sabe que su nombre le viene por la película ‘Gladiator’. ¿Cuántas veces la ha visto? RESPUESTA. La he visto unas cuantas, la verdad. No sé cuántas, pero bastantes; en los aviones me gusta verla, me la sé bastante. P. ¿Te la pones para motivarte? R. Bueno, siempre está esa motivación. Al final, motiva. El nombre viene de ahí, entonces le da una motivación. P. Máximo Décimo Meridio y tú lo lograste con tu décima victoria. Quedan cinco carreras, si no se suspende Qatar, con lo que tiene a tiro el récord de más victorias en la categoría (125 y Moto3), que logró David Alonso, con 14. ¿Se puede? R. Hombre, son palabras mayores. Él lo hizo muy bien. Lo veo difícil, pero lo voy a dar todo para que sea así. Yo creo que si estamos concentrados, podemos lograr más victorias. No sé cuántas, pero intentaré que sean unas cuantas más. P. El décimo también es lo que persigue Marc Márquez. ¿Cómo lo ve? ¿Es posible que lo gane? R. Sí, sin ninguna duda. Mentalmente, está más fuerte que nunca. Físicamente, no tanto por el hombro, pero ya saca él el talento, así que lo veo fuerte y está con ganas. P. ¿Qué te dijo exactamente para felicitarte? R. Al final, él me ha felicitado por el campeonato del mundo, por todo el trabajo. Yo también estoy contento con él por la parte que él ha hecho conmigo. Siempre es bonito que se logre un título y él estaba muy feliz por todo. P. Siempre te preguntamos qué consejos te da Marc. Yo te pregunto: ¿Qué consejos le das tú a él? R. No, yo no me atrevo. Es que en los grandes premios no lo veo. Él tiene su movida; yo, la mía y estamos concentrados. P. Tu próximo reto es Moto2. No tiene ningún test hasta febrero. ¿Te gustaría subirte antes? R. La verdad es que me gustaría antes, pero así la coges aún con más ganas. No sé ni cómo va eso de los entrenamientos ni cuándo puedo hacerlo, pero bueno, cuando tenga que ser, me subiré. P. Tú eres un piloto al que no le importa crear expectativas altas, decir que le va a ir bien desde el principio en Moto2. ¿Por qué? R. Bueno, no lo sé. No me he subido todavía. Es muy difícil, a la gente le cuesta. Es la categoría más difícil, yo diría. Va a ser difícil el comienzo. Habrá que estar muy concentrado, trabajar con el equipo y con todo y ya irán saliendo las cosas. Supongo que irá todo bien y podré dar buenas guerras. P. Marc, estos días, decía que te ha ido todo muy rodado en el Mundial, que no iba mal si pasabas por momentos difíciles para valorar otras cosas y sacar otra motivación. ¿Qué te parece? R. Sí que he pasado por momentos difíciles. Al final, en Inglaterra me lesioné, en mitad de temporada, en un momento importante. Volví y volví a ganar. Todos esos momentos que han sido difíciles; luego, en los entrenamientos, que hay cosas que no se ven, estoy sufriendo y me toca sacar de otros sitios. Eso no se ve, pero está ahí siempre. Siempre hay momentos difíciles. P. ¿Por qué eres tan ambicioso? R. Yo tengo expectativas bajas, normalmente. Antes de los fines de semana, yo me pongo expectativas bajas. Siempre digo que no sé cómo va a ir ahí. Las expectativas son bajas, pero cuando sé que puedo tenerlas altas, las tengo altas. P. Pero tú no te cortas al decir que vas a aspirar a cosas grandes, que van a llegar cosas grandes. R. Sí, es que no puedo decir que no. No he venido aquí a pasarme al Mundial y a ganar un título y ya está. Yo quiero ir a por más. Entonces, siempre son altas, pero es para lo que he venido, para conseguir cosas grandes y lo daré todo para intentar conseguirlo. Son altas, pero en los momentos que toca, tengo las expectativas bajas. P. Has demostrado que llevas la presión bastante bien, ¿no? R. Sí. Siempre está la presión. La realidad es que la presión a veces te hace cometer errores; a mí me ha hecho cometer errores de vez en cuando. Está bien tenerla, pero tampoco mucho tiempo, si no te satura mucho. P. ¿Llegarás a rodar en la misma categoría, en MotoGP, con Marc? Está difícil, porque él firmo dos años y a ti, en teoría, te quedan dos en Moto2, ¿no? R. Nunca se sabe. A lo mejor él se ve inspirado y quiere hacer más años y apuntar a más títulos; no lo sé. O a lo mejor yo llego y subo. Yo voy a estar centrado en mis objetivos, hacer mis años en Moto2, con cabeza, intentar no sufrir tanto, porque será difícil y ya está. P. En MotoGP te deberías encontrar con otro murciano joven: Pedro Acosta. ¿Te ves luchando con él muchos años? R. Vamos a ir paso a paso. Todavía estoy en Moto3, me quedan dos años en Moto2; él ya está haciendo cosas grandes en MotoGP y viene también gente muy joven. Ahora, van a subir a MotoGP Dani (Holgado), David (Alonso), Izan (Guevara)... muchos pilotos muy rápidos. Entonces, habrá que ver cómo se dan de palos ellos y ojalá yo también llegue y esté al nivel de lograr victorias. P. Y por debajo también vienen: Brian Uriarte, Carlos Cano, Álvaro Lucas... R. Sí, hay cantera murciana y española. Se van a cansar de nosotros, de vernos ahí arriba a los españoles. P. En su día, Aspar premió a Pecco Bagnaia, cuando estaba en Moto3, con dejarle rodar con una MotoGP. ¿Te gustaría que te dieran un premio así? R. ¿Sí? No lo sabía. El problema está en que Aspar ahora no tiene equipo en MotoGP, si no ya lo hubiese dicho yo. Me encantaría, por supuesto, pero vamos a ir paso a paso. De momento, en cada momento lo que toque y ya veremos. P. Bueno. Álex Márquez también llevó una Honda y Marc tiene unas cuantas. ¿Te podía dejar alguna algún día? R. Uff. Peligroso. Igual la estrellaría. P. ¿Te gustaría alguna moto en concreto de MotoGP para cuando llegues? R. Eso es lejano. No lo sé. Si el día de mañana, tengo que subir y la moto que funciona ahora no funciona... No se piensa eso. Yo tengo que ir año a año. En Moto2, ahora tengo un objetivo grande, va a ser difícil. No pienso en eso, cuando tenga que llegar, llegará. P. Aquella prueba de Bagnaia llegó por una apuesta de Pecco con Gino Borsoi. ¿Tú te había hecho alguna apuesta por si ganabas el título de Moto3? R. Sí, algo hay, con CFMoto, también, algún buggy. Les dije que si ganaba el título que me dieran un buggy. Hay cosas. P. ¿Y promesas? ¿Habías hecho alguna promesa por si ganabas el título? R. Yo, no, pero dentro del equipo hay promesas que se hicieron entre ellos. Dani Barba fuma y habló con un amigo que si ganaba, tenía que dejar de fumar; ahora va a tener que hacerlo. Hay cosas.

articles.title: Lewis Hamilton: Has trust broken down between Ferrari driver and team's pit wall after Singapore GP issues?
articles.summary: Listen to the latest episode of The F1 Show podcast as Simon Lazenby, Bernie Collins and Karun Chandhok look back at all the big talking points from the Singapore Sprint weekend; watch every session of the United States GP in Austin on October 23-25, live on Sky Sports F1
articles.body:
Hamilton finished finish sixth instead of a likely third in last Sunday's race after not heeding a call from the team's pit wall to stop under a lap-39 Virtual Safety Car.

On team radio after the race following his struggle on worn tyres, Hamilton apologised for "my call" around the strategy, a position he subsequently reiterated on social media when he admitted he had learned a "painful lesson" by choosing "a strategy that ultimately didn't deliver".

It was the second weekend in a row that post-race debate around Ferrari had centred on race strategy.

At the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia the week before, Ferrari's drivers slipped to the back of the field in the twice-delayed race's early stages after the team had been among those to make the mistake of starting on slick tyres when the track was too wet.

Hamilton later said the process around that call, which he had questioned at the time, had prompted a "huge discussion" after the race .

Hamilton eventually fought back to an impressive third place at Sepang after deciding to stay on the slicks longer than team-mate Charles Leclerc, a gamble aided by the timely appearance of the Safety Car as the track dried.

So after further issues in Singapore, this time with Hamilton overriding Ferrari's request to pit under the VSC, the latest edition of the The F1 Show podcast included analysis on the situation at the Scuderia...

Has trust broken down over strategy calls?

Sky Sports F1's Bernie Collins, a former head of race strategy at Aston Martin, was first asked whether Singapore was evidence that the trust between Hamilton and the Ferrari pit wall had broken down.

"Lewis started on the medium tyre, which is one of the things he actually came out and said he thought in hindsight was the wrong decision, but was his decision," said Collins.

"He decided to go that way strategically at the beginning of the race.

"He stops earlier than everybody else so instantly when we're watching at home, we're thinking, 'okay, he's probably on a two-stop here' because he's the first of any of the cars really to stop.

"He puts on that soft tyre. Then they get this perfect opportunity with the virtual safety car to stop again, take another set of soft tyres. You could see the soft was a better tyre and you could see that it was going to be much faster to put a new set on.

"On the coverage at home, we didn't hear any call from Ferrari to box Lewis, but we don't hear a lot of the calls that happen. Fred [Vasseur] obviously came out afterwards and said, yes, they did call him, Lewis missed the entry or ignored the call, whichever way you want to think about it.

"But someone of Lewis's stature doesn't forget to do a pit stop. So let's say it's a decision to not take the pit entry or the call didn't come in time or whatever. But that was crucial, I think, to the race at that point.

"If we go back a week, we had the same sort of lack of trust, for want of another word, in Malaysia."

After Ferrari's tyre choice at the start in Malaysia saw their drivers fall more than a minute off the lead, Hamilton's decision from the car to cut their losses and wait it out on the slicks ultimately paid dividends.

Collins added: "That shows, more globally, that Lewis isn't trusting that Ferrari team.

"He's questioning their decisions and in this sort of quick-decision VSC moment, there's not the time to have all the back and forth about what he thinks or why he thinks it or doesn't think it.

"But it's very difficult from a pit wall and Lewis's side to then think, 'okay, last week I questioned them. I think I was correct. This week I'm going to question them, maybe I'm correct or incorrect.'

"And then there was opportunity later on, I think, even after they missed the VSC, to do a full pit stop and still be able to beat Piastri and they didn't take that either.

"There was the decision then to string it out and hope for another safety car.

"There were lots of decisions that should have been done differently and they should be having a very difficult conversation between Lewis and his engineers, or the strategy team or Fred [Vasseur], whoever needs to be involved, to say, 'where is the trust?

'When we make these decisions, what is the protocol for how that decision is taken and why?'"

Do Ferrari need to give Hamilton more information in the car earlier?

Collins believes that, generally, drivers do need to defer to the pit wall around such decisions given a team's strategists have a fuller picture of what is going on in the race.

However, she used an example from her time at Aston Martin with four-time world champion Sebastian Vettel as showing how teams can also give drivers more information leading up to pit stops.

"In my opinion, yes, [drivers] should [defer to the pit wall]," said Collins. "They're the people with the most information. They're the people with the big picture.

"However, there's another band of thought that says the driver is the most expensive sensor in the car. And I often had situations with Sebastian Vettel, who was very strong strategically, where we ended up starting to give him pit stop information earlier than we would give another driver in order to give him a sort of right to reply.

"If your driver regularly questions strategy, then you need to maybe give them the information.

"Many teams, lots and lots of teams in the situation that Ferrari were in, five laps before the safety car would have said, 'if there's a safety car now, we will take it and double stack the cars'. And that gives Lewis a chance to say, 'I think that's right, I think that's wrong'.

"You've a bit of a discussion about it. Yes, you're giving away information to other teams, which people don't want to do, but you're making the right decision for you and that is your P1 goal. So they need to bring the conversation forward if there's going to be a back and forth."

What are the lessons for both Hamilton and Ferrari?

Fellow Sky Sports F1 pundit and former driver Karun Chandhok believes "they've got to have some sort of reset" in terms of how they approach strategy discussions and decisions at Ferrari.

"Lewis was annoyed with the way Ferrari played that whole race," said Chandhok.

"If you look at it, he started on the medium tyre. Of the top-seven finishers, he was the only one to start on the medium tyre, yet he pitted first. They were clearly unhappy with his pace on the medium. We know it was a less preferred tyre, so they tried to get him off that tyre quickly. Fine.

"But then you have to look at the overall race time and they didn't look at that. They put him out behind Leclerc and then he sat there getting annoyed [at] the fact that he's not getting past Leclerc, and they didn't explain to either driver, that they need a swap. They didn't do a good job in that phase of the race.

"So then you've got Lewis who's now three seconds behind Charles annoyed that he's not been allowed to get in front. The VSC comes out, Charles boxes and he thinks, 'well, I'm going to have free air. I'm going to go for it.'

"He's not thinking of the big picture of the race and that's why I think the strategy team needed to say to him, 'Lewis, your tyres are 21 laps old now, you are going to get passed. You're going to drop like a stone when it comes to pace with all these people.'

"Leclerc didn't have new soft tyres but he had a set that had done one run in qualy, and you could just see, he came out of the pits and was two seconds a lap faster than Lewis when the VSC cleared.

"And that's where any driver has to trust and believe their strategy team and take the inputs and make that decision. But, equally, it's on the team to explain the big picture to the driver and navigate the whole thing and I don't think Ferrari did a good job across the whole race there."

articles.title: Formula 1: Red Bull's Laurent Mekies has contract extended to 2031
articles.summary: Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies, who replaced Christian Horner at the F1 team, has his contract extended until the end of 2031.
articles.body:
Red Bull have extended the contract of team principal Laurent Mekies until the end of 2031.

The Frenchman has led the team since he replaced Christian Horner following the Briton's sacking in the summer of 2025 after 20 years in charge.

After a difficult start to the 2026 season, Red Bull have improved their car to the extent that Max Verstappen has taken dominant victories in the last two races, in Malaysia and Singapore.

A statement attributed to the two main shareholders of Red Bull, Thai Chalerm Yoovidhya and Austrian Mark Mateschitz, said: "Laurent has played a crucial role in guiding the team through an important period of transition while maintaining the competitive spirit and the Red Bull principles that define us.

"This extension reflects our confidence in his leadership and our shared belief in the long-term vision of the team.

"We are ambitious about what lies ahead and we are committed to building on this momentum together."

The move comes less than two months after Verstappen extended his own contract with Red Bull by two years to the end of 2030 after a period of uncertainty over his future.

Verstappen's two victories came in the wake of an interview Horner gave to the Times in which he claimed Red Bull had "lost its mojo, its presence, its vibe".

Oliver Mintzlaff, who is in charge of the Red Bull F1 programme in his role as chief executive officer of corporate projects and investments, said: "Laurent has demonstrated outstanding leadership since returning to the Red Bull family. He combines technical expertise, strategic thinking, and a deep understanding of what makes our team successful.

"Just as importantly, he embodies the values and mentality that define the Red Bull way: courage, teamwork, determination, and an unrelenting desire to compete at the highest level.

"Continuity in leadership is a key ingredient for sustained success."

Mekies said: "I am incredibly proud to continue this journey with Red Bull Racing, and I would like to thank Chalerm, Mark, and Oliver, the entire team, and everyone involved for the trust they have placed in the project.

"What makes this team special is the way everyone comes together in pursuit of the same goal, and I feel privileged to work alongside such a talent and committed group every day."

articles.title: Laurent Mekies: Red Bull team principal signs contract extension to 2031 and vows recent wins 'only the beginning'
articles.summary: Red Bull announce extended five-year contract for team boss Laurent Mekies, who replaced Christian Horner in the role last season; watch every session of the United States GP in Austin on October 23-25, live on Sky Sports F1
articles.body:
Mekies joined the team from sister outfit Racing Bulls in July 2025 after Christian Horner was sacked following 20 years in charge.

News of Mekies' contract renewal comes in the wake of Red Bull claiming their first two wins of the season, both courtesy of Max Verstappen, over the past fortnight in Malaysia and Singapore.

They are fourth in the Constructors' Championship but have closed to within seven points of third-placed McLaren in what is shaping up to be a very competitive end to their first year as an engine manufacturer.

Verstappen extended his Red Bull contract to 2030 in August, while Isack Hadjar was also handed a contract renewal into 2027 after impressing in his first season at Milton Keynes.

In a joint statement announcing Mekies' extended deal, Red Bull shareholders Chalerm Yoovidhya and Mark Mateschitz said: "The strength of Red Bull has always come from its people and from creating an environment where talented individuals can achieve extraordinary things together.

"Laurent has played a crucial role in guiding the team through an important period of transition while maintaining the competitive spirit and the Red Bull principles that define us.

"This extension reflects our confidence in his leadership and our shared belief in the long term vision of the team.

"We are ambitious about what lies ahead and we are committed to building on this momentum together."

Mekies, who has also previously worked at Ferrari and the FIA, said: "I am incredibly proud to continue this journey with Oracle Red Bull Racing, and I would like to thank Chalerm, Mark, and Oliver [Mintzlaff], the entire team, and everyone involved for the trust they have placed in the project.

"What makes this team special is the way everyone comes together in pursuit of the same goal, and I feel privileged to work alongside such a talented and committed group every day.

"Together, with Pierre Wache's and Ben Hodgkinson's teams playing a central role in shaping our future, we have a strong platform for the years ahead, and we genuinely believe this is only the beginning.

"As we look ahead, we will continue to embrace the principles that define us: being free in our thinking, fast in our actions and bold in our decisions."

Oliver Mintzlaff, Red Bull's CEO of corporate projects and investments, also hailed the 49-year-old's Mekies' leadership qualities.

"Laurent has demonstrated outstanding leadership since returning to the Red Bull family," he said.

"He combines technical expertise, strategic thinking, and a deep understanding of what makes our team successful. Just as importantly, he embodies the values and mentality that define the Red Bull way: courage, teamwork, determination, and an unrelenting desire to compete at the highest level.

"Continuity in leadership is a key ingredient for sustained success, and we are delighted that Laurent will continue to lead the team through the next chapter of our journey."

articles.title: NASCAR Announces Last-Minute Rule Change Ahead of Phoenix Cup Series Race
articles.summary: NASCAR announced a rule change Wednesday allowing Cup Series teams to replace front brake pads and rotors at Phoenix Raceway following recent brake failures...
articles.body:
With the NASCAR Cup Series championship battle heating up, officials are making a significant change to the rules just days before Sunday's race at Phoenix Raceway.

NASCAR announced Wednesday , Oct. 14, that teams will be permitted to replace their front brake pads and rotors following Saturday's practice and qualifying sessions. The adjustment comes after a string of brake-related problems raised concerns about what could happen when the series returned to another demanding short oval.

It's an unusual exception to NASCAR's normal post-qualifying restrictions, and one that could help prevent a mechanical failure from derailing a driver's championship hopes.

NASCAR Responds to Brake Concerns Ahead of Phoenix

Brake durability has become a growing concern this season, particularly at tracks where drivers repeatedly slow their cars from high speeds.

The issue was especially noticeable at World Wide Technology Raceway on Sept. 13, when multiple Cup Series cars experienced brake failures during the Enjoy Illinois 300.

Phoenix presents a similar challenge. Its relatively flat, 1-mile layout requires heavy braking, and the Cup Series' increased horsepower package has added another variable for teams to manage.

NASCAR Cup Series Senior Managing Director Brad Moran explained the decision Wednesday on SiriusXM NASCAR Radio's "The Morning Drive."

"We've elected that we're gonna let the teams at least look at their brakes and if they need to make a pad change, which is uncommon for us to do on an impound practice," Moran said. "But we've got a procedure set up to do that."

The permission comes with specific limits. Teams can replace front brake pads and rotors after Saturday's on-track sessions, but no other brake system components may be changed under the exception.

NASCAR will also allow teams to inspect their rear rotors during Sunday's pre-race adjustment period. Any issues discovered during those inspections will be handled individually.

What the New Brake Rule Means for Sunday's NASCAR Race

Importantly, NASCAR isn't requiring teams to make any changes. It's giving them the option.

Moran said there won't be a minimum wear threshold or other specific criteria that teams must meet before replacing their front brake components.

"There's no limit," Moran said. "If a team chooses to change their brake pads, it's on them to do so. The teams are allowed to do quite a bit of work in the brake area. We're just giving the opportunity to make sure they get it right and hopefully we don't have any brake issues at Phoenix."

The timing matters for more than just safety.

Sunday's race is the seventh of 10 events in NASCAR's 2026 Chase for the Cup, with Kyle Larson holding a 49-point advantage over Denny Hamlin in the championship standings.

With only four races remaining, a brake failure could have major implications for drivers trying to close that gap.

NASCAR's decision gives teams an additional opportunity to address potential trouble before the green flag rather than discovering a problem after the race begins.

The Cup Series returns to Phoenix Raceway on Sunday, Oct. 18, with the race scheduled for 3 p.m. ET on USA Network and HBO Max.

articles.title: Brexton Busch, 11, Burned the Tires Off RCR's Parked No. 8 at Kyle Busch's Charlotte Celebration of Life

articles.body:
Richard Childress Racing's No. 8 ran on a Cup car again on Oct. 9 at Charlotte Motor Speedway, for about as long as it takes to destroy a set of tires, and the driver was 11 years old.

Brexton Busch started his late father's No. 8 Lucas Oil Chevrolet, waved to the grandstand and lit up the rear tires near pit entry until there was little Goodyear left. NASCAR.com's account says he then climbed onto the roof, took a checkered flag from his 4-year-old sister, Lennix, and gave the crowd Kyle Busch's post-win bow before jumping down to hug his mother and sister. It was the first time Brexton had publicly driven a Cup car, according to the same report.

That number had been off the Cup grid since May 22. The day after Busch died, RCR announced it would suspend the No. 8 and enter the car as the No. 33, saying the 8 was "reserved and ready for Brexton Busch when he is ready to go NASCAR racing." The team's statement credited Busch with helping design RCR's stylized 8.

Busch was 41. The joint statement from his family, RCR and NASCAR on May 21 called the death sudden and gave no cause. Two days later the family said severe pneumonia had progressed into sepsis.

The celebration began around 8 p.m. at the start/finish line, after Layne Riggs won the Craftsman Truck Series race, and was free to anyone at the track . WBTV reported thousands of fans stayed, and that they were handed Busch flags and rally towels. FS1 carried it live, NASCAR on FOX's Mike Joy hosted, and ten of Busch's cars were parked on display. It followed months of smaller gestures, from an empty chair at Daytona to Rowdy Road at Las Vegas Motor Speedway .

Kurt Busch, who recently bought back his 2000 Roush race truck at Mecum Nashville , opened. "I knew he was going to be fast," he said, per WBTV, describing a younger brother who wanted to do everything "bigger, better and faster than me."

Joe Gibbs, whose No. 18 Toyota Busch drove from 2008 through 2022 to two Cup titles and 56 wins, spoke, as did three drivers who came through Kyle Busch Motorsports' truck program: Daniel Suárez, Noah Gragson and Christopher Bell. Kyle Larson, the defending Cup champion, said Busch called him "Tiny Kyle" and later asked him to help coach Brexton on dirt.

Austin Dillon, Busch's teammate at RCR, kept his short: "Trophies collect dust. Records are meant to be broken."

Samantha Busch said her husband was happy at home through the winless last stretch of his Cup career, and told the grandstand, "This is not the end of Kyle's story." Country singer Cole Swindell played an acoustic set. A drone show drew the No. 18 and the number 234, Busch's win total across NASCAR's three national series, over the track where he won more than any other driver.

Richard Childress was there; NASCAR's photo gallery shows him watching. He wasn't on the speaker list, and nobody announced anything about the car his team holds for Brexton. NASCAR's coverage doesn't say whether the Chevrolet Brexton drove was a race chassis or a show car.

Nowhere in 2027, on RCR's own paperwork. On Aug. 24 the team named Austin Hill full-time driver of the No. 33 for next season, the car he has driven since the Coca-Cola 600. The renumbered entry is now a fixture, not a fill-in.

Childress went further at Michigan in June. He said the No. 8 is reserved for Brexton if he reaches the Cup Series, whether or not he drives for RCR, and that the team had planned to announce a contract extension for Busch before he died. "That kid can drive a race car," Childress said.

Neither RCR nor NASCAR has put a date on any of it, and the rulebook sets its own clock. When NASCAR lowered the O'Reilly Auto Parts Series minimum age last November, it landed at 17 for road courses and shorter ovals and 18 for the big ones. Brexton is about six years from the first of those, and the Cup Series sits a rung above that.

The next public stop is the NASCAR Hall of Fame, where the "Kyle Busch: Honoring A Legacy" exhibit is built around his 2015 championship No. 18 Camry. Samantha, Brexton and Lennix posed with that car at the unveiling. The Hall hasn't said how long the exhibit will stay up.

Should RCR leave the No. 8 parked for however many years it takes Brexton to get there, or put it back on a race car before then?

Sources: Busch family, RCR and NASCAR joint statement (May 21, 2026); RCR No. 8/No. 33 announcement (May 22, 2026); Richard Childress press conference at Michigan (June 6, 2026); RCR Austin Hill announcement (Aug. 24, 2026); NASCAR celebration of life announcement (Oct. 2, 2026), event report, video and photo gallery (Oct. 9 and 10, 2026); NASCAR O'Reilly Series eligibility rule change (Nov. 1, 2025); WBTV.
